module

public import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Pointwise.Finset.Basic

@[expose] public section

/-! # Difference bases

A *difference basis* for a finite set $S$ is a finite set $A$ such that every element of $S$
can be written as a difference $a - b$ of two elements $a, b \in A$; equivalently $S \subseteq A - A$.
The multiplicative version is a *ratio basis* ($S \subseteq A / A$).

The classical case $S = \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ (or $\mathbb{N}$) recovers the notion
of a *restricted difference basis*, dual to the recreational notion of a *sparse ruler*: a
difference basis for $\{0, \ldots, N\}$ of minimal size is an optimal ruler of length $N$.

## Main definitions

* `Finset.IsRatioBasis A S` (additive: `Finset.IsDifferenceBasis A S`): $S \subseteq A / A$.

## Main results

* `Finset.isRatioBasis_iff`: the elementwise characterization.
* `Finset.IsRatioBasis.mono_left` / `Finset.IsRatioBasis.mono_right`: monotonicity.
* `Finset.IsRatioBasis.card_le_sq`: a ratio basis for $S$ has at least $\sqrt{|S|}$ elements,
  i.e. $|S| \le |A|^2$.

## References

- [Wi63] Wichmann, B. "A note on restricted difference bases." Journal of the London
  Mathematical Society 38 (1963): 465-466.
-/

open scoped Pointwise

namespace Finset
variable {G : Type*} [DecidableEq G] [Div G] {A B S T : Finset G}

/-- A finset $A$ is a *ratio basis* for $S$ if every element of $S$ is a ratio $a / b$ of two
elements $a, b \in A$, i.e. $S \subseteq A / A$. -/
@[to_additive IsDifferenceBasis
/-- A finset $A$ is a *difference basis* for $S$ if every element of $S$ is a difference $a - b$
of two elements $a, b \in A$, i.e. $S \subseteq A - A$. -/]
def IsRatioBasis (A S : Finset G) : Prop := S ⊆ A / A

/-- A finset $A$ is a ratio basis for $S$ iff every $x \in S$ is a ratio of two elements of $A$. -/
@[to_additive isDifferenceBasis_iff
/-- A finset $A$ is a difference basis for $S$ iff every $x \in S$ is a difference of two elements
of $A$. -/]
theorem isRatioBasis_iff : IsRatioBasis A S ↔ ∀ x ∈ S, ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, a / b = x := by
  simp only [IsRatioBasis, subset_iff, mem_div]

/-- Shrinking the target set preserves being a ratio basis. -/
@[to_additive /-- Shrinking the target set preserves being a difference basis. -/]
theorem IsRatioBasis.mono_left (h : IsRatioBasis A S) (hTS : T ⊆ S) : IsRatioBasis A T :=
  hTS.trans h

/-- Enlarging the basis preserves being a ratio basis. -/
@[to_additive /-- Enlarging the basis preserves being a difference basis. -/]
theorem IsRatioBasis.mono_right (h : IsRatioBasis A S) (hAB : A ⊆ B) : IsRatioBasis B S :=
  h.trans (div_subset_div hAB hAB)

/-- A ratio basis for $S$ has at least $\sqrt{|S|}$ elements: $|S| \le |A|^2$. -/
@[to_additive /-- A difference basis for $S$ has at least $\sqrt{|S|}$ elements: $|S| \le |A|^2$. -/]
theorem IsRatioBasis.card_le_sq (h : IsRatioBasis A S) : S.card ≤ A.card ^ 2 :=
  calc S.card ≤ (A / A).card := card_le_card h
    _ ≤ A.card * A.card := card_div_le
    _ = A.card ^ 2 := (pow_two _).symm

end Finset

findings.description: The module docstring at lines 28–30 says that taking S = {0,…,N} recovers a restricted difference basis. This specialization of Finset.IsDifferenceBasis only requires S ⊆ A − A; it does not restrict the locations of A's elements. For example, Lean verifies that A = {0,1,3} is a difference basis for {0,1,2}, although A is not contained in that interval. The generic definition itself is correct; the claimed specialization in the documentation is not.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/170 explicitly requires both A ⊆ {0,1,…,N} and {0,1,…,N} ⊆ A−A, and separately mentions the question 'without the restriction A ⊆ {0,1,…,N}'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_ruler likewise distinguishes unrestricted n-perfect rulers from complete rulers whose endpoints are 0 and N.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep Finset.IsDifferenceBasis unchanged. Amend the module paragraph to say that imposing A ⊆ {0,…,N} in addition to IsDifferenceBasis gives a restricted difference basis, equivalently a complete ruler of length N.

findings.description: Independently of the missing interval restriction, line 30 identifies minimum cardinality at a fixed length with an 'optimal ruler'. In the terminology used by the sources and by SparseRuler.IsOptimal, this gives a minimal ruler, not necessarily an optimal one: optimality also requires maximal length for that number of marks. For example, {0,1,2} is minimal for length 2, but {0,1,3} is a longer complete ruler with the same three marks. The scratch file proves SparseRuler.IsMinimal [1,1] and ¬ SparseRuler.IsOptimal [1,1].
findings.source_evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_ruler defines a minimal ruler by minimum marks at fixed length, a maximal ruler by maximum length at fixed marks, and says: 'A sparse ruler is called optimal if it is both minimal and maximal.' Peter Luschny's introduction also distinguishes these notions: https://web.archive.org/web/20210330141047/http://www.luschny.de/math/rulers/introe.html .
findings.suggested_fix: After adding the interval restriction, replace 'an optimal ruler of length N' with 'a minimal complete ruler of length N'. Alternatively, explicitly add maximality at the fixed number of marks before calling the ruler optimal.

findings.description: In the direct consumer FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/SparseRuler.lean, the explanatory text at lines 28–31 and 93–96 gives an incomplete list of exceptions to the all-rulers classification and miscounts the segments of the length-58 examples. A known non-Wichmann optimal ruler has marks {0,1,2,8,15,16,26,36,46,56,59,63,65,68}: it has length 68 and 13 segments, yet 68 is omitted. The listed length-58 examples have 13 marks, hence 12 segments, not 13. This is a documentation error, not an error in the theorem's 13 < g.length bound. Lean checks that the displayed length-68 gap list is complete and is neither a Wichmann gap list nor its reversal.
findings.source_evidence: https://oeis.org/wiki/User:Peter_Luschny/PerfectRulers, section 'Wichmann rulers', explicitly displays this length-68 ruler R alongside W(2,3), states that both are optimal, and identifies R as the non-Wichmann example in the following section. That section states the exact stronger conjecture: 'All optimal rulers with more than 13 segments are either Wichmann rulers or the mirror images of Wichmann rulers.' The Wikipedia examples table records 13 marks for length 58.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct the exception discussion, preferably by citing Luschny's exact stronger conjecture and the length-68, 13-segment example motivating the cutoff. Remove or correct the purported exhaustive length list, and change the segment count for length 58 to 12. No change to the Lean theorem is needed.

reformulations.difference: On natural-number inputs, the definition uses truncated Nat subtraction rather than integer subtraction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any finite A,S ⊆ ℕ, this is equivalent to applying the integer difference-basis predicate to their images in ℤ. A positive equation a − b = k forces a ≥ b, so truncation has no effect. For k = 0, any truncated witness can be replaced by the diagonal pair (a,a). The converse follows immediately from the integer difference equation. This equivalence was proved for arbitrary A and S, including empty sets and zero.

reformulations.difference: The consumer applies the unrestricted difference-basis predicate without an explicit hypothesis that its basis lies in the interval from 0 to the ruler length.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every natural-number partial sum of g lies between 0 and g.sum, and the index range includes both the empty prefix and the full prefix. Thus marks g automatically contains both endpoints and lies in Finset.range (g.sum + 1). Together with the difference characterization, this gives IsComplete g ↔ marks g ∈ Erdos170.PerfectRulersLengthN g.sum. This exact iff was proved, including g = [].

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement quantifies over List ℕ without separately requiring positive gaps, whereas the source uses strictly increasing marks.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Minimality excludes zero gaps: filtering them out preserves the marks, total length, and completeness, but strictly decreases the list length if any zero occurs. This implication was proved in Lean. Allowing zero-containing competitors also does not change either extremum: remove zeros for the minimum comparison; for a purported longer maximum competitor with fewer distinct marks, add unused integer marks until the required number is reached. There is room because its length exceeds that of the positive-gap ruler. Consequently the predicates express the source's extrema on genuine rulers. The resulting >13-segment classification is explicitly stated by Luschny. The full source-to-Lean iff was not formalized.
